title: Repairing a concrete doorstep edge with repair mortar
subtitle: Rebuild a broken or spalled concrete doorstep edge using a polymer-modified repair mortar bonded to the existing concrete
excerpt: How to repair a broken, crumbling, or spalled front edge on a concrete doorstep using polymer repair mortar. Covers cleaning the damage, applying a bonding agent, mixing and applying the mortar, and shaping the finished repair.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade practice for concrete repair and polymer-modified mortar application.

glossaryTerms.definition: A factory-blended polymer-modified mortar used to rebuild damaged concrete. It bonds to existing concrete through a bonding agent and is more flexible than plain sand-and-cement, reducing the risk of the repair cracking away from the substrate.

The breaking away of the concrete surface in flakes or chunks, caused by water freezing in the concrete pores, reinforcement corrosion, or weak original mix. A spalled edge has crumbling surface concrete with the aggregate exposed or absent.

content.text: A broken or spalled concrete doorstep edge is rebuilt with a polymer-modified repair mortar applied over a bonding agent. The mortar is shaped while plastic and sets hard within 24 hours. BEGINNER: no specialist tools are needed, and the mortar is forgiving on timing.
Break away all loose or crumbling concrete from the

area. The repair will not bond to loose material: tap along the damaged zone with a cold chisel handle and knock away anything that sounds hollow. The remaining concrete must be solid. Clean out dust, dirt, and loose aggregate with a stiff brush and a vacuum. Wet the concrete surface and allow to become just damp, not saturated, before applying the bonding agent.

Brush a liberal coat of PVA bonding agent onto the repair surface. Allow to dry until tacky: this takes 10 to 20 minutes depending on the temperature. Apply the repair mortar while the bonding agent is still sticky. If the agent dries completely, apply a second coat and use that.

to a stiff paste according to the manufacturer's instructions. Press the first layer firmly onto the bonded surface, working it into any undercutting. For repairs deeper than 25 mm, apply in two layers, scratching the first layer before it sets to give a key for the second.

Use the plasterers trowel to build the mortar slightly proud of the finished level, then scrape back flush with the surrounding concrete. Form the front arris (the corner of the step nose) with the edge of the trowel or filling knife, running the tool along the edge in one smooth pass. Cover the repair with a polythene bag or damp cloth for 24 hours to slow the cure and reduce cracking.

attrs.symptom: Repair crumbles away from the step within a few weeks
attrs.cause: The bonding agent was not applied, had dried fully before the mortar was applied, or the substrate concrete was not cleaned.
attrs.fix: Remove all loose repair material, clean the surface, apply bonding agent, and relay while tacky. Ensure the substrate is damp before applying agent.

attrs.symptom: Surface cracks appear across the repair while curing
attrs.cause: The mortar dried too fast in hot or windy weather.
attrs.fix: Keep the repair covered with a damp cloth for the first 24 hours and avoid applying in direct sun. Hairline cracks can be filled with concrete sealant.
